issues.legal_issue: An officer conducting a public-ferry auction may reject the highest bid only by exercising the statutory discretion on relevant material and considering the prescribed factors.
material_facts: A public ferry was auctioned, and the first respondent made the highest bid.
The officer awarded the ferry to a lower bidder, recording only that the two higher bidders appeared on a government-maintained special list.
The officer did not independently assess material about the highest bidder or consider the prescribed factors before rejecting his bid.
The highest bidder had previously been prosecuted for a prohibition offence but was discharged.
issues.conclusion: The rejection of the highest bid was not in accordance with the governing Act and rule because the officer had no relevant material on which to exercise the discretion and rejected the bid solely because the bidder appeared on the special list.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8 of the Northern India Ferries Act, 1878, and rule 19 framed under section 12, a ferry sale should generally go to the highest bidder, although the officer may reject that bid for sufficient reasons recorded in writing. The discretion is wide but not unrestricted: the officer must consider the factors specified in rule 19 and act on relevant material. A court will not reverse a properly exercised discretion, but rejection without material supporting it is non-compliance with the rule.

rule.if: public_ferry_auction and highest_bid_rejected and officer_relied_only_on_special_list and not officer_assessed_relevant_material

predicates.public_ferry_auction: An officer conducted a public auction to settle the tolls or lease of a public ferry.
predicates.highest_bid_rejected: The officer rejected the bidder who offered the highest bid.
predicates.officer_relied_only_on_special_list: The officer rejected the highest bid solely because the bidder appeared on a government-maintained list of suspected or confirmed wrongdoers.
predicates.officer_assessed_relevant_material: The officer independently assessed relevant material about the bidder and considered the factors applicable to the decision.

issues.definition: When a public-ferry auction’s highest bid is rejected solely because the bidder appears on a special list and the officer has not assessed relevant material, the rejection is unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: A confidential government list of suspected or confirmed involvement in wrongdoing, whose sources and preparation process are undisclosed, is not a sufficient evidentiary basis by itself for deciding a person’s civil rights.
material_facts: The officer rejected the highest bidder because his name appeared on a confidential government list of persons suspected or confirmed to be connected with smuggling.
The list did not disclose the information or sources on which it was prepared or the procedure used to compile it.
The bidder’s earlier prosecution had ended in his discharge.
The list was relied on to decide who would receive the ferry settlement.
issues.conclusion: The special list was not a document falling within section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and it was unsafe to rely on the list alone to decide civil rights or reject the bidder.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, did not apply to the special list. Although such lists might guide criminal intelligence work, a list whose sources and method of preparation are undisclosed is unsafe as the sole basis for deciding civil rights.

predicates.civil_rights_decision: An authority used information to decide a person's entitlement to a civil benefit or right.
predicates.government_list_used_as_sole_basis: The authority relied only on a government-maintained list to make that decision.
predicates.list_sources_and_compilation_process_und: The list did not reveal the sources of its information or how it was prepared.

issues.definition: A government list with undisclosed sources and preparation methods is insufficient by itself when an authority uses it to decide civil rights.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may not itself make a discretionary settlement entrusted by law to an executive authority, even when the authority’s original decision was unlawful.
material_facts: The governing law entrusted the decision on whether to accept a bid and settle the ferry to executive authorities.
The High Court set aside the settlement to the lower bidder and declared that the highest bidder was entitled to the settlement.
The Supreme Court held that the executive authorities, rather than the court, had to make the settlement decision.
The lease concerned a period that was shortly due to expire, so the Supreme Court considered that a fresh decision by the authorities was unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred insofar as it declared the highest bidder entitled to the settlement; the decision was for the appropriate executive authorities. Because the lease period was shortly expiring, the Supreme Court did not direct fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Where legislation entrusts a discretionary decision to executive authorities, a court reviewing the decision may set aside an unlawful order but may not itself decide the matter entrusted to those authorities. The Court followed Verappa Pillai v. Raman & Raman Ltd., [1952] S.C.R. 583.

predicates.judicial_review_of_executive_settlement: A court is reviewing an executive authority's decision about a settlement or comparable allocation.
predicates.law_entrusts_discretion_to_executive: The governing law assigns the discretionary decision to an executive authority.
predicates.court_declares_entitlement_instead_of_le: The court itself declares who is entitled to the settlement rather than leaving the decision to the responsible authority.

issues.definition: When a law assigns a discretionary settlement decision to an executive authority, a reviewing court cannot itself declare who is entitled to that settlement.
